props.title: Working Girl

sections.content: Working Girl (1988) brilliantly captures the late-80s Wall Street zeitgeist through a female lens, offering a sharp contrast to male-dominated films like Wall Street (1987). Melanie Griffith's Tess McGill embodies the struggle of ambitious working-class women fighting against classist assumptions and sexual harassment. The film's portrayal of corporate Manhattan - from the Staten Island Ferry commute to the glass-and-steel offices - creates a perfect backdrop for this modern Cinderella story that subverts expectations by emphasizing Tess's business acumen over romance.

sections.content: The film's exploration of female mentorship and betrayal through Sigourney Weaver's Katharine Parker character created a template for subsequent workplace dramas. Unlike Disclosure (1994) or Fatal Attraction (1987), Working Girl avoids demonizing career women, instead showing how systemic inequalities pit women against each other. Harrison Ford's Jack Trainer serves the unusual role of romantic lead who supports rather than rescues the protagonist, marking a significant shift from traditional romantic comedy dynamics.

Director Mike Nichols, fresh from success with Heartburn (1986), brings his signature mix of comedy and social commentary to illuminate class divisions. The film's Oscar-nominated screenplay by Kevin Wade expertly weaves corporate intrigue with personal ambition, while Carly Simon's "Let the River Run" became an anthem of female empowerment, winning both Academy Award and Golden Globe for Best Original Song. SUBHEAD: Class and Gender in 1980s Corporate America

sections.content: Working Girl emerged during a pivotal moment in films about workplace gender dynamics. While Fatal Attraction (1987) portrayed career women as dangerous threats and Big Business (1988) played corporate culture for broad comedy, Nichols' film tackled serious issues of class mobility and gender discrimination while maintaining optimistic humor. The film's influence can be seen in later works like In Good Company (2004) and Morning Glory (2010), which similarly explore workplace hierarchies through a generational lens.
